In all such partly verbal, partly nonverbal kinds of rhetorical devices, the nonverbal element also persuades by reason of its symbolic character. Paper need not know the meaning of fire in order to burn. But in the "idea" offire there is a persuasive ingredient. By this route something of the rhetorical motive comes to lurk in every "meaning" however purely "scientific" its pretensions. Wherever there is persuasion, there is rhetoric. And wherever there is "meaning," there is "persuasion." Food, eaten and digested, is not rhetorical. But in the meaning o[food there is much rhetoric, the meaning being persuasive enough for the idea of food to be used, like the ideas ofreligion, as a rhetorical device of statesmen. (RM 172-73)

This passage seems far from clear. Additionally, the numerous ironizing quotation marks and italics indicate various forms of pressure and stress. The word meaning, not insignificantly, is italicized twice and twice placed in quotation marks. What does meaning mean here? The most direct reading would be that Burke understands meaning to emerge as our ideas about the world, making meaning the sense or significance of things, events, and relations. Meaning is gleaned from the symbolicity that drapes over (or maybe permeates) the mundane world, circulating it as the significance available to us. The mention of science is important here, for Burke is clearly dissatisfied with a positivist, scientific claim of mere facticity for things of the world, as if measuring qualia sufficed for generating meaning. Thus, he will grant that paper, being paper, has no ideas as such; its rapid oxidation at temperatures around 451 degrees Fahrenheit is a purely chemical reaction. But to remain at this level is to willfully (or methodologically) remain at observation degree zero, and it obscures fire's role in human affairs. When Bradbury's Fireman comes to

burn the books, though, we move into a different realm, one of meaning, and we see that fire is a full rhetorical participant. Fire, then, is more than just a sensed material phenomenon; its integration into the human world necessitates ideas. These ideas mean, and insofar as they mean, they bodily invoke, and insofar as they bodily invoke, they persuade.

As I observed in my discussion of Hawhee, this is not an abstract notion of fire as meaningful; rather, it is one entirely grounded in the bodily integration of ideas stemming from physical experience. As Burke puts it in Attitudes toward History, "our primeval ancestors, by learning language, no longer experienced a sensation solely as a sensation" (382). As he goes on to explain, we may like the warmth ofa fire, and such warmth is certainly a sensation, but as soon as we start putting such experience into language, the words come to "tell a story"; as a result, attitudes (or affective stances) can emerge and be deployed across various forms of discursive interaction, such as the movement from "that feels warm" to the observation that someone is "warm-hearted" (Burke,AH383).

This elevation of meaning over mundane, objective matter is further evinced in other passages. Later in A Rhetoric of Motives Burke again discusses the effect of material phenomena. This time he calls them a form of intuition, and he then tethers intuition to a notion of infancy. One can perceive a seashell, for instance, and note the generative regularity of its spiral. but without more firmly and robustly grasping the intelligibility of that spiral in the world of human meaning, such as reasoning out the mathematical functions that generate various spirals, such an encounter remains stuck in what he terms "infancy," a notion he further compares to the "realm of the unconscious in dreams" (RM 174-75). But before we begin complaining about the terribly slanted and problematic valuation here, where conscious reason trumps infantile intuition, we must see the antistrophe he proposes immediately thereafter. An "intuition" of spring is not a mere passive perception, a datum of sensory (or even supersensory) knowledge. My arguments for the importance of ambience should not be understood as any simple call to "pay attention." One is in any event only partially aware of ongoing events within one's environs at any given time. The environs are ready-to-hand, yes, but they now have agentive powers Heidegger's hammer never had. Emile A arts and Stefano Marzano point out, "As technology becomes hidden within these static, unintelligent objects, they will become subjects, active and intelligent actors in our environment ... [and the] immaterial world of our interactions with them-services, games, entertainment, information, communication-will become more prominent in our lives" (8-9). Greenfield argues that ubiquitous computing "will disturb unwritten agreements about workspace and homespace, the presentation of self and the right to privacy. It contains an inherent, unsettling potential for panoptical surveillance, regulation, and 'rationalization.' Its presence in our lives will transfigure our notions of space and time, self and other, citizen and society in ways we haven't begun to contemplate" (3). In short, ambient intelligence radically changes who we are in our environs; it

situates us differently in the world, evoking other ways of being. It thereby also reveals rhetoric to us differently than it has appeared heretofore. Ambience thus teaches us that we cannot rely solely on salience, attention, and consciousness to guide us.

Rhetoric has much to learn from music on this score. I am claiming that ambient music is an important development, both in its own right as a form of thinking (and not simply as expression ofhuman thought and affect) and as something that shows how the power of place and the agency of technology become integral not just to the music's creation but to what we take the music to be. Music is not just the salience of its affective work. Ambient music has still other rhetorical dimensions, including politics. It has ramifications for how we dwell in the world. Eno claims that ambient music is directly political: "The decision to stop seeing yourself as the centre of the world, to see yourself as part of the greater flow of things, as having limited options and responsibility for your actions[.] ... that is political theory: and it's where the music grows from" (qtd. in Tamm 91).

It is hardly a stretch to see that these political insights resonate with the extension of digital computing into things and environs. As Eno is quite aware, there are both opportunities and dangers here, which is why transforming how one sees oneself in the world is integral to a politics attuned to these dangers. 21 So, much as ambient music does, ubiquitous computing (ambient intelligence) showcases how the power of place and the agency of technology become integral not just to our everyday activity but to a conception of dynamic life itself. We need not overstate the case by claiming we are on the threshold of a brave new world. Rather, we are simply seeing capacities, implications, and energies as previously assembled now giving way to vibrant and different intensities and assemblages. But we cannot ignore how these different forms also assemble new forms oflife, or new ways of being-in-the-world.

Rhetoric, Ambience, Dwelling

We need conceptions ofrhetoric that keep pace with these transformations and their attendant opportunities and dangers, that not only help us make sense of them but enable us to flourish (and that will, of course, spur new transformations). We do not need a new rhetoric, however; rather, we must work anew with what has been brought forward in rhetorical theory and practice. Rhetoric is revealing and doing-doing as revealing and revealing as doing-and hence integral to our dwelling in the world. As part of his engagement with technology, the later Heidegger developed a rich notion of dwelling. Dwelling as he uses it entails an ecological attunement to the environment, although it will mean more than this. It differs from, say, the idea that we all have worldviews, which would make dwelling a matter of properly tempering our cultural knowledge. Worldviews, as I have argued, posit a more or less stable common reality variously shaping or shaped by human culture and language. The notion of worldviews invokes the subjective, writ large as society, and thereby gives over to (Western) science the authority to pronounce the truth of nature. A worldview thus constitutes how the world appears "out theren as colored by cultural lenses, a position that insinuates a disengagement between people and world, so that ultimately "objective" reason becomes the means to eliminate cultural distortion and get at the actual essence of things (Ingold 15). 2 As Heidegger argues, however, dwelling indicates not a worldview but a principle of being: culture is materially enworlded. That is, dwelling is a way of being conditioned and permeated by things so that they are inseparable from what it means to live in the world. But dwelling also has a hermeneutic character, in that, like Dasein, questions

of being are continually at issue (see Heidegger, BT 32). The question of how existence is best pursued is not simply given as knowledge but achieved through continual questioning. Such questioning and formulating does not reside solely with the human. Thus, dwelling is not mere survival or existence, nor is it the layering of culture over mundane reality. Dwelling is characterized by thriving or "flourishing" conceived in an ecological key (Heidegger, DT 47). It is not simply an ensemble of practices or habits whose daily performance gets marked by the style we then associate with a particular community. Rather, dwelling indicates lived relations woven into complex ecologies of the world's things and forces. This is not passive coexistence or simple adaptation to things; it is an active if conditioned comportment toward the world. Indeed, this is why Heidegger connects dwelling with building (PLT 146, 148).3By doing so, he grounds human flourishing in constructive activity. That is, the attunement to the world that characterizes dwelling is not passivity. Rather, it is activity that works through and with things as they show up in the world alongside us. Heidegger characterizes this relationship as a dynamic kind of''letting ben appearing as forms of shepherding, cultivating, sparing, and ca retaking (PLT 147-48).

Heidegger's terminology is overly rustic, an important and not unproblematic consideration. Heidegger incorporated such attitudes into much of his thought. When he turned to technological artifacts in his critical ruminations on technology, he often found them to lack a special status he reserved for "things," which were as often as not illustrated through rustic examples. A wine jug is a thing, but a river dam is an object, and in the later Heidegger, the "object" label conveys a negative valuation. I think we must resist this valuation but not simply reject it. Rather, we might ask what stakes lie in making a distinction between a thing and an object. Can this distinction tells us anything that bears on rhetoric and its relation to things and how we dwell with them, even as we move past the limitations we recognize in Heidegger's particular articulation of this distinction? These questions indicate that Heidegger's romanticizations are more than evocations of the rustic. In order to explain this, I want to look at what Heidegger has to say about things and, in particular, how he wants to grant to the thing, as opposed to the object, the ability to manifest what he calls the fourfold (das Geviert). The fourfold is the gathering of earth, sky, mortals, and gods-admittedly a rather oblique statement. Dwelling, Heidegger will argue, is life that takes its bearings from, manifests, and cultivates an attunement to the fourfold. And the fourfold is also characterized by

island, not a resource for the maximization of human uses and profits. In their way oflife they give the island to take part, not to preserve it or to naturalize it, but to cultivate it as part of their homemaking. Indeed, this gets at the essence of dwelling, caring for as a freeing to let something be what it is.14 Rather than utter no to technology or to building, this hearkening brings forth a relation to technology that takes its bearings from the profundity of a holistic ecology, which tempers the will to impose, dominate, or master with the call to care.

The world, thought as material presence, as meaning, and as that which withdraws, is sacralized by everyday practices in such a fashion as to ground meaning and worth beyond the human. Values, ifwe can still risk that term, emerge from these practices and are neither settled nor projected solely by human beings. On this account, if values in this sense transcend human being, then Latour's Dingpolitik must already be spoken in a way oflife. Dwelling gives rise to Dingpolitik, which is to say that there is already something like an ethic implicit in our worldliness. There is no adding on a new comportment toward things, toward world after the fact, as Latour would have it. Indeed, this is the crucial point for understanding why religion, art, and other forms of knowledge are just as important as science or politics; they are already in deep relation to and disclosive for our way of being, for the way we dwell. for ethos. Thus, performing rhetoric in an ambient key is less a matter of adding them back in than of reattuning ourselves to their station, and to what their station may yet be, in our struggle to find better, more sustainable practices. Certainly, their role in knowledge formation and ethics remains vital. But there are other aspects that could be made equally vital. For instance, religion, art, and forms of celebration would be important for their evocation of something like the festive. Festivity need not be happy and chipper, either; the festive is important for attuning us to the gifting of the world and a sense of value that transcends human being, manifest through moods of contemplation, reverence, joy, or other possibilities.15 Such celebration is also a form of preparatory rhetoric, since it discloses world differently and opens the possibility of dwelling anew. That is, art, religion, and other ways of being with things would allow them to show up for us as things that are indispensable for our way oflife and for the being of world in general: they are radiant in such fashion that they are graced to us and so lay claims on us should we listen to them. 16 Note that this aligns with Latour's and Heidegger's claims that science is not the sole source for knowledge about things. One need not

accede to antiscience religious doxa to uphold the idea that science is not the last instance for determining the knowledge that enlivens our everyday being. The festive is one way to pursue this enlivening.

Although I find the Toronto Islanders' resistance to the automobile important and illuminating, it is important not to romanticize their efforts, as if the island's residents have found an ideal path that we should then imitate. Not only is it difficult to transport practices that are so wedded to the region, since the specificity of place is an integral element in those practices, but it is far from assured that they have succeeded. Indeed, I have spent a good amount oftime explicating where they struggle. Nevertheless, we cannot neglect the rhetorical potency of arguments such as Princen's or practices such as those of the Toronto Island residents. I have stated that they are only preparatory, and I want to close on that note. Such preparation lays the groundwork necessary for awakening attunements that in turn give rise to other forms of disclosure and receptivity. That is, thought in terms of an ambient rhetoric, such preparatory work is crucial, for it brings us in touch with the world's primordial affectability, and disclosing this transforms how world comes to us in a way that shifts our manner of being in that world. This suggests that this book itself is ultimately only preparatory. Perhaps this too is necessary. An ambient rhetoric cannot trump itself, cannot short-circuit itself into being a new paradigm. That would run counter to its disclosive power for rhetoric itself. When it comes to world making, an ambient rhetoric can only attune and, by such attunements, conjoin us in worldly affectability giving place and bearing to everything we are and everything we do.

Movement, Heidegger's Silence, Disclosure

Dwelling, then, entails more than existing and subsisting; it extends beyond simply doing what we need to do-working, socializing, building-to survive to include the richness that is developed and pursued in how we are doing so. Building is not just construction, notjust technics. Nor is it isolable, except at cost, from ambient concerns. To understand place in terms of building necessitates the fullest possible understanding of what makes a location a location. As Heidegger goes on to explain, the fourfold is already wrought with the building of the farmhouse, since the building ofit, which sprang from dwelling, is already a located response to and a living with the fourfold. The farmhouse is built from and sustained by what the earth gives

and lies nestled in the earth's hollows; it receives its direction and temporality from the sky and is further sustained by what the sky brings; the divinities are traced in thankfulness and respect, fear and hope; and death and birth and all the cares of mortals are knit into the house and responsive to the other three aspects of the fourfold, as each of the others similarly join together. None of these things is present in any simple and direct manner. but they can all be seen as gathered in the way of life that gave rise to the farmhouse. Thus, the fourfold cannot be reduced to direct presence, as it is also what remains concealed, although we too often take the mundane persistence of presence as all there is, since it is most near to our everyday concerns. Place is never given in its entirety.

But here we come to the crucial point. This withdrawing is also a form of supporting; it is the repletion of all that is, which in turn ensures that the world is always more than what we make ofit. If the world is to make claims ,on us, ifwe are to dwell in such manner as to attune ourselves to what is noninstrumental. nonrepresentational, then this withdrawal becomes es- :sential. In other words, human knowledge is al ways only partial, and rather tha1\ see this as an invitation to extend knowledge further, as ifwe could pry open all mystery and have it stand revealed before us, Heidegger argues that what remains unconcealed is itself valuable. Dwelling makes being's concealment an occasion for joy and humbleness, thought and insight, guidance and action. It grants the world a kind of meaning or value that, while it cannot speak directly (and hence is neither meaning nor value, exactly), nevertheless calls us in its holding sway and conditions every aspect of our being together. This is the productive "acknowledgment of what is not human in the context of what is" (Thiele, Timely 179). Thus, a location is inseparable from its unique expanse and its ecological connectedness to larger surroundings; all take part in making place a place. Human building arises from place, of course, and is a further disclosure of place, but Heidegger seems to indicate that there is something sound and hale in attuning ourselves to place's role in our constructive pursuits rather than seeking only human-derived, technical, or efficiency-driven projects. I will explore this idea further in the next chapter.

So far I have been arguing that dwelling and the fourfold grant insight into an originary affectability materialized in things and in the world's worlding. This, however, is precisely what renders advertising, or at least much of it, shrill. Forms of rhetoric that disclose the world and place human beings as resources for maximizing advantage, as most advertising does, eschew or foreclose the rich ecological relationality of being-in-the-world. That is, such forms deattune us. One cannot simply castigate this move. of course. One ought not simply say that advertising is wrong or evil, nor am I making any such argument. But neither should we ignore how advertising can convey narrowly suasive aspects of our being to disproportionally outsize all others, like eating nothing but cake all day. Other ambient variables that could condition advertising in its specific messages (you need cheap tacos at 2 a.m. !) or larger sayings (Consume!) are dimmed. This dimming contributes simultaneously to advertising's power and to our phenomenological reaction to it as shrill, as too sweet. A diet of advertising is unsustainable. And for this reason, while advertising is rhetoric, neither good nor ill, it would be an error to posit it as illuminating rhetoric's basic principle. Of course, this is precisely what, say, philosophy commonly does: thinly slice rhetoric as a manipulative version of persuasion, so that we see its shrillest forms as constituting its primary essence. A "sustainable" rhetoric (I discuss sustainability and sufficiency in chapters 7 and 8) is one that brings us to the richer experiences already spoken through language's saying, not solely as a sign system, but as the ch orographic background resounding of our attunement to the world.in

Heidegger's theory oflanguage allows us to rethink rhetoric as persuasion so as to take it out of a delimiting subject/object framework. Persuasion is certainly an affordance of rhetorical interaction, but an ambient perspective lets us see that taking rhetoric as persuasion narrowly and subjectively defined deflects our emplacement in the background "relation of all relations" that is language and distances us from the conditioning sway of the nonhuman that also gives place and bearing to rhetoric (Heidegger, OWL 135). Rhetoric emerges from our being-in-the-world, then, precisely also as a response to the way the world attunes and speaks us, but a response that allows for new forms of revealing that transform, at least potentially, how we are in relation to the world. This grants that even ifwe keep rhetoric always within language's orbit, language is never simply the doing of human beings, so that the wellspring of what rhetoric is and can be is opened through an attunement to its ambience. That is, rhetoric not only

receives its bearings from an attunement to all aspects of worldly existence that give rise to ways of being, human and nonhuman, but does so without mistaking any given presencing as ultimate being. Rhetoric thereby shares in a partiality that, rather than limits us, offers us hope for further and enriching unfoldings in rhetorical being.

The Rhetorical Thing

Only when man becomes the subject do non-human beings become objects.

Rhetoric has always dealt with things, which is to say that rhetoric has not ignored the material realm. The field's historically predominant focus on rhetor, audience, and language may obscure this point, but contemporary rhetorical theory in particular attends to materiality. For instance, the field has firmly incorporated Marx's notion of dialectical materialism and its attendant critique of ideology. In addition, substantial contemporary work has investigated technology, institutions, and bodies. Indeed, even the notion of materiality is increasingly thematized in its own right as worthy of direct scholarly attention (Biesecker and Lucaites, Kochin). But the problem has always been how and to what extent materiality itself matters. As a long tradition has had it, rhetoric, being one of the seven liberal arts and crucial for the formation of what we call the humanities, is most fundamentally an affair of human beings and their dealings. This, then, is the perplexing issue. If Princen's narrative about the potential of rhetoric is only preparatory for dwelling as sufficiency, particularly given environmentalism's track record so far, perhaps the issue is not just one ofrhetoric's persuasive scope and power. Princen's argument is convincing; his ability to distil the logics of efficiency and sufficiency, superior; his call for moving to sufficiency, compelling. To say this, of course, already keeps to a certain notion ofrhetoric and hence already becomes part of what is at issue. In other words, to grapple with sufficiency requires questioning how we conceive rhetoric itself. The sophistication of Princen's understanding of sufficiency is undone by the subjective and epistemological conception of rhetoric on which he relies, one that is coterminous with his presentation of sufficiency as a logic. It is still a matter of a rhetor addressing an audience in a social and discursive context, or a realm of experts and politicians with the power to change a few social practices that can induce better, more ecologically minded choices. Yet even in the midst of this rhetorical problematic, we can see glimmers of a deeper understanding of what has to be done. One of the more perspicacious moments in the book comes when Princen quotes Andrew Rudin, an energy-management specialist, who says: "it's not the car engine, it's the roads and the parking and the speed limits and the status of walking and bicycling and busing. It's not the speed of the message, it's the combination of e-mail, fax, telephone, and postal mail. It's not the productivity of the farms, it's the food networkH (qtd. in Princen 109). The real matter at issue is never just one given problem but how that problem is threaded through an entire array of knowledges, practices, discourses, organizations, and things. Rudin's remark traces the extent to which sustainability is not a social problem requiring discursive or policy solutions but rather a problem ofan entire way oflife materialized in practices and things and a conception ofrhetoric that has the materiality of dwelling built in.

This idea connects back to Heidegger's argument (see chap. 5) that what appears to us is ultimately not just a singular object but an ensemble of interlocking and interacting elements. We are immersed in an environment that surrounds, structures, affords, and sustains. I demonstrated this with Heidegger's example of the Black Forest farmhouse. To understand the

farmhouse is not to isolate it and pinpoint its features but rather to unravel the complex mutual conditioning of people, things, actions, and environs as they combine to give rise to homemaking, how the various actants "receive directives" from and mutually sustain one another (Heidegger, PLT 158). This is the essence of dwelling. And as I have been arguing, this rich notion of dwelling has much to give to rhetorical theory. Dwelling places us in the insight that rhetoric, being worldly, cannot be understood solely as human doing and that persuasion gains its bearings from an affectability that emerges with our material environments both prior to and alongside the human. An ambient approach no longer sees rhetoric as a direct extension of human will or human meaning making. Thus the commonplace understanding ofrhetoric as a discursive exchange between contextually arranged but otherwise disparate rhetorical agents falters. Instead, we need to see that rhetoric emerges from the ambient environs, the in which and from which that give it its bearings and thrust it forward. Ifwe retain rhetoric's traditional notion of context, it is stretched far beyond its delimitation as a social-discursive situation to include a vibrant materiality, such that rhetoric is not just played out in an environment but embedded complexly in and through it.

The importance Heidegger places on world thus transforms the locus of agency. This transformation occurs not only through argument but through Heidegger's terminology and syntax. In his translation of Ontology, John van Buren explains that many of Heidegger's verbs, including begegnen (to encounter), are best understood in a middle voice that muddles or even reverses the subject-object relationship: with Heidegger, a phrase that might customarily be translated as "the world is something we encounter" would more accurately be rendered as "the world is what en-counters (us)" (0 118n53).13 In his study of the problem of the will in Heidegger's thought. Bret Davis argues that Heidegger often uses this middle voice at decisive points to convey "an 'activity' prior to or other than that which can be articulated in a subject/predicate grammar and a subject/object ontology" (15-16). From his earliest to his late writings, such grammatical and terminological

constructions abound, including also the sort of"verbing" that sounds tautological: "the world worlds," "the thing things," or most infamously, "the nothing nothings" (B. Davis 16).

Heidegger's most famous book.Being and Time.lays out the situatedness (Befindlichkeit) of Dasein in an ontological framework with great nuance and detail. While place and environment are important here, we should look again to Heidegger's discussion ofattunement, or mood. Attunement or mood is ontological and primordial, meaning it precedes all cognition and volition (BT175). Mood "assails us," arising"out ofBeing-in-the-world, as a way of such Being," so that "the mood has already disclosed, in every case, Being-in-the-world as a whole, and makes it possible first of all to direct itself towards something" (BT 176). For instance, something in the environment appears as threatening only because Dasein is attuned to fearfulness (BT176). Affect is a modality of the entanglement of world and body. Indeed, this attention to attunement/mood leads to Heidegger's praise of Aristotle's Rhetoric as "the first systematic hermeneutic of the everydayness of Being with one another" (BT 178). Importantly, current studies in neuroscience can be seen as empirically verifying Heidegger's philosophical claims (see Ratcliffe). Mood is not reducible to psychological or conscious cognitive states, to "interior" phenomena, since it is constitutively entangled within and emerges from the environment in which we are situated and therefore also is a prerequisite for intelligibility as such (Ratcliffe 289). 14 Still, the extended mind perspective of cognitive science has not always attended to affective states as much as it should, although recent work by Damasio and others is certainly starting to have wide impact. But it is worth emphasizing that the phenomenological concept of Befindlichkeit as worked out by Heidegger through attunement/rnood does emphasize feeling and emotion, and in this and other ways, cognitive science still has much to gain from an engagement with Heidegger (see Ciborra). Finally, as Daniel Gross demonstrates, Heidegger makes a contribution to rhetoric in emphasizing that pathos is the ground oflogos, not vice versa. In his 1924 seminar on Aristotle, Heidegger states, "insofar as the pathe are not the annex of psychical processes, but are rather the ground out of which speaking arises, and which what is expressed grows back into, the pathe, for their part, are the basic possibilities in which being-there [Dasein] itself is primarily oriented toward itself. finds itself' (BCAP 176; transliterations added). Indeed, Gross remarks, here we have "[a] world seen and prefigured by the pat he" (Gross, "Being-Theren 38; see also Greenspan and Shanker). On this account, then, feelings, whether they are socially refracted and circulated emotions or the

more deep-seated moods characterizing how we find ourselves, are neither subsidiary to human existence nor an impediment to rational activity. Rather, they are fundamental. This remains an extremely important point for rhetorical study and practice.
